questions.question: Explain how development is defined and measured, covering the growth-development distinction, the economic and social indicators with their weaknesses, and the two spatial models with a fair criticism of each use.
questions.expected_answer: Development is improvement in the quality of human lives, not merely growth — which is more output countable in currency; development asks whether output becomes health, schooling, choice and dignity. Economic indicators: GDP values everything produced inside a country in a year, GNI the income of a country's people and firms wherever earned, both usually per capita to compare countries of different sizes — but as averages they are silent about distribution. The Gini coefficient measures that gap, from zero at perfect equality toward one at total concentration, and South Africa's score is among the highest recorded anywhere. Social indicators reach where money cannot: life expectancy, infant mortality — the most sensitive single test of living conditions — literacy, and access to safe water and sanitation. The HDI folds a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living into one score between zero and one; its lesson is that equal incomes can produce unequal HDI because policy decides whether money becomes clinics and classrooms. Spatially, core-periphery explains unevenness within and between countries — Gauteng as core accumulating investment and skills, the former homelands as periphery exporting labour and receiving remittances, the pattern repeating at world, country and city scale. Rostow's five stages — traditional society, preconditions, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption — supply a vocabulary but must be criticised: the model assumes every economy climbs the West's staircase, ignores colonial history and late-starter handicaps, and treats arrival as guaranteed.

questions.question: Analyse how the rules of trade disadvantage raw exporters and evaluate the aid debate, defining the key terms and reaching a balanced conclusion.
questions.expected_answer: The founding pattern is colonial: the periphery exports primary products — ores, crops, crude — and imports manufactures. Primary prices lurch and drift downward against manufactured prices, so the terms of trade — export prices against import prices — slide against raw exporters: the same trainload of ore buys fewer machines every year. The escape is beneficiation and industrialisation — processing materials at home to capture value added, selling jewellery rather than raw gold — the value-chain climb East Asia demonstrated through export-led growth. Key terms: balance of trade is goods exported minus imported; free trade removes barriers while protectionism raises tariffs, quotas and subsidies — with the standing grievance that wealthy countries subsidise their own farmers while preaching open markets; globalisation integrates markets and has lifted hundreds of millions but concentrates power in multinationals and transmits distant shocks; South Africa trades through BRICS and the African Continental Free Trade Area while shedding the minerals-out, machines-in dependency. Aid types: humanitarian or emergency; development aid; technical assistance; multilateral through bodies like the World Bank against bilateral state-to-state; and tied aid wrapped in donor strings. For aid: it saves lives, builds clinics, schools and dams beyond the budget, transfers skills, and at its best — vaccination, the HIV campaign — transforms societies. Against: dependency when donated goods undercut local producers, leakage to corruption, tied aid serving the donor, and the 1980s-1990s debt trap. Balanced conclusion: aid works when it builds capacity and answers locally set priorities — and fair trade and investment cure more than charity.

questions.question: Assess South Africa's energy mix and the state of its soil through the lens of sustainability, ending with the circle that connects development, energy, climate and soil across the year.
questions.expected_answer: Over four-fifths of electricity is coal-fired from stations standing on the Mpumalanga seams: coal milled and burned, steam raised, turbine and generator spun, waste heat exhaled by the cooling towers. Coal is cheap, local, job-rich and delivers baseload, but its charge sheet holds heavy per-person carbon emissions, Highveld air pollution, gigalitres of scarce water, scarred land and acid mine drainage. Koeberg's nuclear is low-carbon and steady but costly, slow and burdened with centuries of waste; hydro is small in a river-poor country, partly imported from Cahora Bassa, while pumped storage at Drakensberg and Ingula serves as a water battery, not a source. Non-conventional energy exploits a world-class endowment: Northern Cape photovoltaic and concentrated solar plants banking heat in molten salt, and Eastern and Western Cape wind farms — built through competitive procurement rounds that drove prices below new coal — but intermittency requires storage, backup and grid, and coal towns require a just transition. Soil forms over centuries and is lost in single storms — effectively non-renewable — with only about 12 per cent of land arable and 3 per cent high-potential against losses of several hundred million tonnes a year; the erosion ladder runs bare ground, splash, sheet, rill, gully, and the remedies run it backward: cover, contour ploughing, terracing, rotation, carrying capacity and gabions. Sustainability — meeting present needs without compromising future generations — is the banking rule: live off interest, never capital; coal is capital burning, sun and wind are interest arriving. The circle: development needs energy; coal energy spends water and warms the climate; the loaded climate delivers droughts and storms; storms strip bare soil into dongas; lost soil starves the farming development promised to feed. The way out applies the toolkit at every join — renewable power, protected soil, value-capturing trade, capacity-building aid — with responsibilities assigned to government, business and individuals.
